title: How to Grow From Senior to Staff Engineer in the AI Era
author: Gregor Ojstersek et al.
summary: Gregor Ojstersek and co-authors use Jordan Cutler's trajectory at Pinterest as a case study for the senior-to-staff engineer transition in the AI era, arguing that the shift is not primarily technical but dimensional: it requires expanding from individual depth to three simultaneous dimensions -- broader surface area, cross-team influence, and systems designed for scale. Surface area expansion is the most immediately visible dimension: staff engineers are expected to understand and affect systems and teams beyond their immediate codebase. This does not mean becoming a generalist but becoming a technical leader whose decisions account for architectural implications across multiple teams and systems. Cross-team influence is the leadership dimension: staff engineers must move other engineers not through authority but through technical credibility and communication. This requires the ability to frame technical decisions in terms of business impact and to build coalitions across teams with competing priorities. In the AI era specifically, the staff engineer role expands to include AI system design: understanding where AI amplifies team output and where it introduces failure modes at scale. Staff engineers who can reason about AI leverage points -- where automation is reliable enough to deploy widely and where it requires human judgment -- have a qualitatively different value proposition.
points: The senior-to-staff transition is primarily a dimensional shift rather than a technical deepening: it requires expanding from single-team depth to organisation-wide surface area, cross-team influence, and architectural thinking at scale.

Cross-team influence -- moving engineers outside your own team through technical credibility and communication rather than authority -- is the core leadership competency of the staff role and cannot be substituted by technical excellence alone.

In the AI era, staff engineers must develop a distinct meta-skill: identifying where AI leverage is reliable enough to deploy at scale versus where it introduces failure modes requiring human oversight -- a judgment call with major architectural consequences.
Jordan Cutler's Pinterest trajectory illustrates that the bottleneck to staff promotion is rarely technical skill but almost always documented track record of cross-team impact.
The scalable systems dimension requires staff engineers to design for the organisation's future state -- anticipating growth, failure modes, and the teams who will inherit the system.
quotes: This week's newsletter is a collaboration with Jordan Cutler, a Staff Engineer at Pinterest, who shares the specific moves he made to grow from Senior to Staff in the AI era -- and the three dimensions that separate the two roles.

The senior engineer optimises within a defined scope. The staff engineer redefines the scope. That reframing is not semantic. It changes what you read, who you talk to, which meetings matter, and how you evaluate your own success.

Cross-team influence is the competency that most senior engineers underestimate and most staff engineers name as decisive. You cannot move into the staff role on technical depth alone. You must be able to move people who have no reason to follow you.

In the AI era, the staff engineer's most important judgment is not which model to use. It is where human judgment remains load-bearing and where it can be safely delegated to a system. Get that wrong at scale and the failure is architectural, not just technical.

Jordan's inflection point at Pinterest was not a brilliant technical insight. It was the moment he started framing his technical recommendations in terms their business stakeholders could evaluate -- and discovered that this translation was itself a form of technical leadership.

Scalable systems are not just systems that handle more traffic. They are systems that can be understood, modified, and extended by engineers who were not in the room when they were designed. Designing for that constraint is a staff-level skill.
